{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=memory+experience+preference+formation+path+dependence&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"A correlational study of animation narrative style preferences, viewing behavior, and audience experience.\", \"abstract\": \"

Introduction

The association between animation narrative styles and the audience's psychological experience is a critical question in media psychology. Grounded in Uses and Gratifications (U&G), this cross-sectional correlational study examines how narrative preferences are associated with viewing experience.

Methods

Through a survey of 615 animation viewers, we evaluated how complex/non-linear, coherent/linear, and visual/expressive preferences correlate with cognitive engagement and flow experience. K-Means cluster analysis was utilized for audience segmentation.

Results

Two significant \\\"preference-experience\\\" pathways emerged: a positive correlation between a preference for complexity and cognitive engagement, and a strong correlation between a preference for coherence and flow experience. Furthermore, viewers were clustered into Analytical Viewers, Casual Plot-Followers, and Indifferent Viewers. Cognitive engagement exhibited a statistical indirect association between complexity preference and flow experience.

Discussion

These findings supply empirical evidence for understanding audience selection behaviors and offer evidence-bounded implications for content creation and platform recommendation strategies, highlighting an eudaimonic and a hedonic gratification path.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1834298\", \"pmid\": \"42936023\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13699482\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1834298\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13699482\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org…

Grounded in Rogers' diffusion-of-innovations theory, the present study employed a mixed-methods design. Four waves of independent cross-sectional quantitative data (T1-T4, N = 788) were complemented by semi-structured interviews with 20 undergraduate students. Key patterns emerged as follows: (i) Across later waves, the direct association between external regulation and intrinsic motivation attenuated, while the indirect association operating via identified regulation strengthened. The path from identified regulation to intrinsic motivation was the only relationship that demonstrated significant cross-pair differences while satisfying invariance requirements for all three wave-pair comparisons. Because scalar invariance could not be established, this pattern is interpreted solely as a descriptive group-level temporal trend and should not be read as evidence of intra-individual change. (ii) AI-assisted creativity showed the largest and most consistent downward shift: estimates in later waves were significantly lower relative to the T1 baseline, with effect sizes increasing progressively (Δ = -0.391 to -0.549; d = -0.61 to -0.95; all p < 0.001 following Holm correction). This pattern remained largely unchanged after adjusting for gender, year of study, and academic major, and held up in four predefined subsamples as well as under propensity-score weighting. (iii) The linkage between AI dependency and creativity was significantly positive only at T3 and became negative but non-significant at T4, pointing to a conditional, wave-specific association rather than a stable linear relationship. Abstract
Multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) aims to optimize policies in the
presence of conflicting objectives, where linear scalarization is commonly used
to reduce vector-valued returns into scalar signals. While effective for certain
preferences, this approach cannot capture fairness-oriented goals such as Nash
social welfare or max-min fairness, which require nonlinear and non-additive
trade-offs. Although several online algorithms have been proposed for specific
fairness objectives, a unified approach for optimizing nonlinear welfare criteria in
the offline setting—where learning must proceed from a fixed dataset—remains
unexplored. In this work, we present FairDICE, the first offline MORL framework
that directly optimizes nonlinear welfare objective. FairDICE leverages distribution
correction estimation to jointly account for welfare maximization and distributional
regularization, enabling stable and sample-efficient learning without requiring
explicit preference weights or exhaustive weight search. Across multiple offline
benchmarks, FairDICE demonstrates strong fairness-aware performance compared
to existing baselines.
1 Introduction
Sequential decision-making in real-world domains often requires balancing multiple conflicting
objectives, as seen in applications like autonomous driving [1, 2], robotic manipulation [3, 4], and
wireless network resource allocation [5]. Multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) addresses
this challenge by providing a principled framework for learning policies that maximize aggregated
returns over conflicting objectives. While standard MORL with linear scalarization focuses on
maximizing a weighted sum of objective returns, MORL with nonlinear scalarization, or fair MORL,
promotes fair outcomes through concave scalarization objectives, such as Nash social welfare [6].

title: Learning with AMIGo: Adversarially Motivated Intrinsic Goals
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2006.12122v2
published: 2020-06-22T10:22:08Z
summary: A key challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) consists of learning in environments with sparse extrinsic rewards. In contrast to current RL methods, humans are able to learn new skills with little or no reward by using various forms of intrinsic motivation. We propose AMIGo, a novel agent incorporating -- as form of meta-learning -- a goal-generating teacher that proposes Adversarially Motivated Intrinsic Goals to train a goal-conditioned "student" policy in the absence of (or alongside) environment reward.
